title: Chapter XXIX
paragraphs: The evening after the funeral, my young mistress and I sat in the library, sometimes dwelling sorrowfully—one of us hopelessly—on our loss, sometimes daring to speculate about the dark future ahead.

We had just agreed that the best Catherine could hope for was permission to stay at the Grange, at least while Linton lived, with him allowed to join her and me to remain as housekeeper. It seemed almost too favourable an arrangement to hope for. Yet I did hope, and began to take comfort in the prospect of keeping my home and work, and above all my beloved young mistress. Just then a servant, one of those dismissed but not yet gone, rushed in to say “that devil Heathcliff” was crossing the yard. Should he shut the door in his face?

Even if we had been mad enough to order that, there was no time. He did not trouble to knock or announce himself. He was the master and used the master's privilege of walking straight in without a word. The servant's voice led him to the library. He entered, motioned the man out, and shut the door.

It was the same room into which he had been shown as a guest eighteen years earlier. The same moon shone through the window, and the same autumn landscape lay outside. We had not yet lit a candle, but the whole room was visible, including the portraits on the wall: Mrs. Linton's magnificent head and her husband's graceful one. Heathcliff walked towards the hearth. Time had changed his appearance very little either. He was the same man, his dark face a little more sallow and composed, his body perhaps a stone or two heavier, but otherwise unchanged. At the sight of him, Catherine had jumped up, meaning to rush out.

“Stop!” he said, catching her arm. “No more running away! Where would you go? I've come to take you home. I hope you'll be a dutiful daughter and won't encourage my son to disobey me again. When I discovered his part in the affair, I hardly knew how to punish him. He's such a cobweb that a pinch would destroy him. But you'll see from his face that he's had his due! The evening before last I brought him downstairs and put him in a chair, and didn't touch him afterwards. I sent Hareton out, so we had the room to ourselves. Two hours later I called Joseph to carry him upstairs again. Since then my presence has affected his nerves as powerfully as a ghost, and I fancy he often sees me when I'm nowhere near. Hareton says he wakes and screams for hours in the night, calling for you to protect him from me. Whether you like your precious husband or not, you must come. He's your responsibility now. I hand over all my concern in him to you.”
“Why not let Catherine stay here,” I pleaded, “and send Master Linton to her? Since you hate them both, you wouldn't miss them. They _must_ be a daily nuisance to that unnatural heart of yours.”

“I'm looking for a tenant for the Grange,” he answered, “and of course I want my children around me. Besides, the girl owes me work for her keep. I'm not going to support her in idleness and luxury after Linton's gone. Hurry up and get ready, now. Don't make me force you.”

“I will,” Catherine said. “Linton is all I have left in the world to love. You've done everything you could to make me hate him and him hate me, but you _can't_ make us hate each other. And I defy you to hurt him while I'm there. I defy you to frighten me!”

“What a boastful defender you are,” Heathcliff replied. “But I don't like you enough to hurt him. You'll have the full benefit of that torment for as long as it lasts. I won't be the one who makes you hate him: his own sweet nature will do that. He's bitter as gall about your desertion and its consequences. Don't expect thanks for this noble devotion. I heard him painting Zillah a pretty picture of what he'd do if he were as strong as me. The will is there, and his very weakness will sharpen his wits to find something to replace strength.”

“I know his nature is bad,” Catherine said. “He's your son. But I'm glad mine is better, so I can forgive it. I know he loves me, and that's why I love him. Mr. Heathcliff, _you_ have _no one_ who loves you. However miserable you make us, we'll still have the revenge of knowing your cruelty comes from being even more miserable yourself. You _are_ miserable, aren't you? Lonely as the devil, and envious like him? _Nobody_ loves you. _Nobody_ will cry when you die! I wouldn't be you!”
She spoke with a bleak sort of triumph. It seemed she had resolved to adopt the spirit of the family she was joining and find pleasure in her enemies' suffering.
“You'll soon be sorry to be yourself,” her father-in-law said, “if you stand there a minute longer. Off with you, witch! Get your things!”

She left with a look of contempt. While she was gone, I began begging to take Zillah's place at the Heights, offering to give up mine to her. He would not hear of it. He ordered me to be quiet, then for the first time let his eyes travel around the room and over the portraits. After studying Mrs. Linton's, he said, “I'll have that taken home. Not that I need it, but—” He turned sharply towards the fire and continued with what, for want of a better word, I must call a smile. “I'll tell you what I did yesterday. The sexton was digging Linton's grave. I got him to clear the earth from her coffin lid, and I opened it. For a moment I thought I'd stay there. When I saw her face again—it's still her face!—he could hardly move me. But he said it would change if the air reached it, so I loosened one side of the coffin and covered it up. Not the side nearest Linton, damn him! I wish he'd been sealed in lead. I bribed the sexton to pull that side away when I'm buried there and slide mine out too—I'll have my coffin made that way. Then by the time Linton reaches us, he won't know which is which!”
“That was very wicked, Mr. Heathcliff!” I exclaimed. “Weren't you ashamed to disturb the dead?”

“I disturbed no one, Nelly,” he replied, “and I brought myself some peace. I'll be much more comfortable now, and you'll have a better chance of keeping me underground once I'm there. Disturb her? No! She's disturbed me, day and night, for eighteen years—without rest, without mercy—until last night. Last night I was at peace. I dreamt I was sleeping my last sleep beside her, my heart stopped and my cheek frozen against hers.”
“And if she'd crumbled into earth, or something worse, what would you have dreamt then?” I asked.

“Of crumbling with her, and being happier still!” he answered. “Do you think I fear any change like that? I expected it when I lifted the lid, but I'm better pleased that it should wait until I can share it. Besides, without that clear impression of her still, untroubled features, I could hardly have shaken off that strange feeling. It began in an odd way. You know how wild I was after her death, praying without end, from dawn to dawn, for her spirit to return to me! I believe strongly in ghosts. I'm convinced they can exist among us, and do! Snow fell on the day she was buried. That evening I went to the churchyard. The wind was bleak as winter, and the place was deserted. I wasn't afraid her fool of a husband would wander up the valley so late, and no one else had any reason to be there. Alone, knowing that only two yards of loose earth stood between us, I said to myself, ‘I'll hold her in my arms again! If she's cold, I'll think it's this north wind chilling _me_. If she doesn't move, she's asleep.’ I fetched a spade from the tool shed and dug with all my strength. It scraped the coffin. I began working with my hands, and the wood started cracking around the screws. I was just about to succeed when I seemed to hear someone sigh above me, bending down close to the edge of the grave. ‘If only I can get this off,’ I muttered, ‘let them shovel the earth over both of us!’ I wrenched at it more desperately than ever. Another sigh came close to my ear. I seemed to feel its warm breath push aside the sleet-filled wind. I knew no living person of flesh and blood was there. But as surely as you sense yourself approaching a solid object in the dark without being able to see it, I felt Cathy there—not beneath me, but above ground. Relief suddenly flowed from my heart through every limb. I abandoned that agonising labour and turned away, instantly comforted—comforted beyond words. Her presence stayed with me while I filled in the grave, and led me home. Laugh if you like, but I was certain I'd see her there. I knew she was with me and couldn't help speaking to her. When I reached the Heights, I rushed eagerly to the door. It was locked. I remember that accursed Earnshaw and my wife trying to keep me out. I remember stopping to kick the breath out of him, then hurrying upstairs to the room that had been mine and hers. I looked impatiently around. I felt her beside me. I could _almost_ see her, and yet I _could not_! I should have sweated blood then from the agony of longing, from the desperate force of my prayers for just one glimpse. I got none. She proved herself a devil to me, as she so often had in life! Since then, more at some times and less at others, I've been the plaything of that unbearable torture. Hellish! It has kept my nerves stretched so tight that, if they hadn't been made of catgut, they would long ago have gone as slack and feeble as Linton's. Sitting in the house with Hareton, I'd feel that if I went out I'd meet her. Walking on the moors, I'd feel I'd meet her when I came in. Whenever I left home I hurried back. She _must_ be somewhere at the Heights; I was certain of it! As for sleeping in her room—I was driven out of that. I couldn't lie there. The moment I closed my eyes she was outside the window, or pushing back the panels, or coming through the door, or even resting her darling head on the same pillow as she used to as a child. I had to open my eyes and look. So I opened and closed them a hundred times a night, always to be disappointed! It tortured me! I've often groaned aloud until that old scoundrel Joseph must have thought my conscience was playing the devil inside me. Now that I've seen her, I'm calmer—a little. What a strange way to kill a man: not by inches, but by fractions of a hair's breadth, luring me on with the ghost of a hope for eighteen years!”

Mr. Heathcliff stopped and wiped his forehead, where his hair clung wet with sweat. His eyes were fixed on the red embers. His eyebrows were not drawn together but raised towards the temples, making his face less grim, yet giving it a peculiar troubled look, a painful appearance of a mind strained towards one all-consuming subject. He was only half speaking to me, and I kept quiet. I did not like hearing him talk! After a short while he returned his attention to the portrait, took it down, and leaned it against the sofa to see it better. While he was occupied with it, Catherine came in and announced that she was ready as soon as her pony was saddled.

“Send that over tomorrow,” Heathcliff told me. Then he turned to her. “You can do without the pony. It's a fine evening, and you won't need ponies at Wuthering Heights. Your own feet will do for any journeys you make. Come along.”
“Goodbye, Ellen,” my dear little mistress whispered. Her lips were icy as she kissed me. “Come and see me, Ellen. Don't forget.”
“Make sure you do nothing of the sort, Mrs. Dean!” said her new father. “When I want to speak to you, I'll come here. I don't want you prying around my house!”

He motioned her ahead of him. With a backward look that cut me to the heart, she obeyed. From the window I watched them go down the garden. Heathcliff tucked Catherine's arm under his, though she clearly resisted at first, and hurried her with long strides into the avenue, where the trees hid them from sight.
